title: Book 6 — Erato, Chapter 59
paragraphs: When many thousands of these and of the Helots and of the Spartans themselves have been gathered together in the same place, with their women intermingled, they beat their foreheads with a will and make lamentation without stint, saying that the one who has died last of their kings was the best of all. Whenever any of their kings has been killed in war, they prepare an image to represent him, laid on a couch with fine coverings, and carry it out to be buried. After the burial, no assembly is held among them for ten days, nor any meeting for the choice of magistrates; but they keep mourning during these days. In another respect too they resemble the Persians: when the king is dead and another is appointed king, this newly incoming king releases any Spartan who was a debtor to the king or to the state—just as among the Persians the new king who comes to the throne remits to all the cities the arrears of tribute due.
